newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU finance ministers not expected to discuss lira.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers not expected to discuss lira.

text.p: European Union finance ministers, fresh from seeing the Finnish markka join the bloc's exchange rate mechanism (ERM), met on Monday as eyes turned to the Italian lira as the next likely candidate for the grid.
But officials said there was very little chance of the ministers discussing the lira in anything more than a passing fashion on Monday.
"The markka is still fresh in people's minds but I don't think there will be any substantive discussion about the lira," one EU diplomat said as ministers arrived for the scheduled meeting.
"It's more likely to be coffee table chatter," he added.

The Finnish markka became the 11th of 15 EU currencies in the ERM on Monday following a decision on Saturday in Brussels by the EU's monetary committee. It will trade at a central rate of 3.04 to the German mark.
The move was seen as giving a boost to EU plans for a single currency in 1999.
Only Britain, Greece, Sweden and Italy are currently outside the ERM grid. Italy, tossed out in a currency crisis in 1992, has said it wants to join again soon.
But EU officials say it will be much harder to bring in the lira than the relatively stable markka. One official said he doubted it could happen before December.
European Commission President Jacques Santer denied that there would be extra pressure on the EU to let in Italy now that they markka was in.
"No pressure," he told reporters, "but Italy is making very good steps in the right direction."

Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink also said there would be no increased pressure on his country to enter the ERM. Sweden, along with Britain, argues that it is not necessary to be in the ERM to qualify for a single currency.
The single currency was not formally on the ministers' agenda. Instead, they were expected to discuss the European Commission's plans for funding Trans-European Networks as a way of creating jobs.

Commission President Jacques Santer has proposed spending an additional 1.0 billion Ecus ($1.26 billion) for the so-called TENs projects. But his plea has consistently fallen on deaf ears, many governments insisting that the money go towards reducing national budget deficits.

With nearly all of the EU's 15 nations engaged in an all-out sprint to meet the Maastricht treaty's tough criteria on budgets and debt for monetary union, EU spending proposals which are considered less than urgent have received scant support.
The road and rail networks were an integral part of Santer's confidence pact for employment, an initiative launched earlier in the year to tackle the union's mounting jobless rate.

The 14 priority projects, indentified by EU leaders at a summit in Essen in December 1994, include high-speed trains between Paris and Cologne and between Frankfurt and London, plus motorways in Greece, Spain and Portugal.
Diplomats said there were widespread expectations the finance ministers would once again reject the TENs funding plan and put an end to the debate.
